mcqs.q: Cleaning, within the biomechanical preparation, is achieved by:
opts: Proper instrumentation together with irrigation and intracanal medication
mcqs.explain: Cleaning plus shaping make up the biomechanical preparation, which with diagnosis and obturation produces endodontic success.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the primary objectives in cleaning and shaping?
opts: Widen the apical foramen to allow irrigant extrusion
Remove infected soft and hard tissue
Give disinfecting irrigants access to the apical canal space
Retain the integrity of radicular structures
mcqs.explain: Creating space for medicaments and obturation is the fourth objective; extruding irrigant through the apex is an accident, not an aim.

mcqs.q: In a cross-section of a prepared canal, the region cleaned by IRRIGANTS versus INSTRUMENTS is:
opts: The instrument reaches a round central core; the irrigant must clean the whole outline
The instrument cleans the whole outline and the irrigant only the core
mcqs.explain: This is precisely why irrigation, not instrumentation, determines the outcome in a complex canal system.

mcqs.q: The MECHANICAL effectiveness of irrigation depends on:
opts: The ability of irrigation to generate optimum streaming forces within the entire root-canal system
The concentration of the antimicrobial irrigant
The area of contact with infected material
The duration of interaction between irrigant and tissue
mcqs.explain: The other three are the determinants of CHEMICAL effectiveness.

mcqs.q: Which belongs to the MECHANICAL AND CHEMICAL objectives of irrigation rather than the biologic one?
mcqs.explain: Lubricating the canal, dissolving organic and inorganic tissue and dealing with the smear layer are the others; the antimicrobial effect is the biologic function.

mcqs.q: According to the AAE Glossary, the smear layer consists of dentin particles, remnants of vital or necrotic pulp tissue, retained irrigant and:
mcqs.explain: It is a surface film of debris retained on dentin after instrumentation with rotary instruments or endodontic files.

mcqs.q: The smear layer is removed in endodontics in order to:
opts: Let irrigants, medicaments and sealers enter the dentinal tubules and improve disinfection
Increase the bond strength of the coronal restoration
mcqs.explain: Note the contrast with operative dentistry, where the smear layer is regarded as moderately protective.

mcqs.q: Which four components inside the root canal system are flushed out by irrigants?
opts: Vital tissue, bacteria, necrotic tissues and dentine debris
Vital tissue, sealer, gutta-percha and bacteria
Necrotic tissue, cementum, enamel and dentine debris
mcqs.explain: Dentine debris is the inorganic component, generated by the instruments themselves.

mcqs.q: The irrigating needle should be placed:
opts: 2 mm shorter than the working length
5 mm shorter than the working length
mcqs.explain: The needle is bent, must lie passively, must never lock in the canal, and 2 ml is delivered each time.

mcqs.q: During irrigation, the needle should:
opts: Lie passively and never lock in the canal
Be wedged firmly so it cannot move
Be held at the canal orifice only
mcqs.explain: A needle that binds leaves no path for backflow, which is how extrusion accidents happen.

mcqs.q: The recommended volume of irrigant at each exchange is:
mcqs.explain: The irrigation should be delivered slowly, with the needle lying passively.

mcqs.q: A 27-gauge needle inserted into a prepared canal:
mcqs.explain: A 30-gauge side-venting needle reaches the apical third, but only in adequately enlarged canals.

mcqs.q: A common 27-gauge injection needle has an external diameter of:
mcqs.explain: Smaller irrigation tips with an external diameter of 0.32 mm are the 30-gauge needles.

mcqs.q: A 30-gauge needle corresponds to which ISO size?
mcqs.explain: 27 gauge is # 40, 25 gauge is # 50, 23 gauge is # 60 and 21 gauge is # 80.

mcqs.q: A 23-gauge needle corresponds to which ISO size?
mcqs.explain: Note that a HIGHER gauge number means a NARROWER needle.

mcqs.q: Compared with large needles, narrow needles:
opts: Require more pressure on the plunger and extrude the irrigant with higher velocity
Require less pressure and give lower velocity
Deliver a greater volume of irrigant
mcqs.explain: Large needles extrude greater amounts of irrigant but cannot be introduced as deep — reach versus volume.

mcqs.q: A side-vented needle is characterised by:
opts: Releasing the solution via lateral openings, with a closed, safe-ended tip
Releasing the solution from an open flat tip
mcqs.explain: The closed end deflects flow sideways instead of jetting it straight at the foramen, which is what makes it safer.

mcqs.q: In the classification of needle tips, which group is OPEN-ended?
mcqs.explain: A–C are the open-ended designs and D–F the closed-ended ones.

mcqs.q: Which is a property of an ideal irrigant?
opts: Stain tooth structure to aid visualisation
mcqs.explain: The ideal irrigant should also be an effective germicide and fungicide, non-irritating, stable in solution, and have a prolonged antimicrobial effect.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the ideal irrigant is correct?
opts: It should be active in the presence of blood, serum and protein derivatives of tissue
It should be inactivated by blood and serum
It should be antigenic to stimulate healing
It should alter the physical properties of exposed dentin
mcqs.explain: It must also be capable of inactivation in a culture medium, so that microbiological sampling remains valid.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT listed among the six types of irrigant?
mcqs.explain: The six are sterile saline, sodium hypochlorite, chlorhexidine, chelating agents (EDTA), MTAD and QMiX.

mcqs.q: Commercial household bleach contains sodium hypochlorite at:
mcqs.explain: It is used in dilution from 0.5% to 5.25% by adding distilled water to lower its toxicity.

mcqs.q: The pH of sodium hypochlorite is:
mcqs.explain: This alkalinity is both the source of its antimicrobial action and the reason it is tissue toxic.

mcqs.q: NaOCl is the irrigant of choice principally because it:
opts: Rapidly dissolves necrotic and vital pulp tissue and the organic components of dentin
Has the greatest substantivity of any irrigant
Is non-toxic to the periapical tissues
mcqs.explain: It is the only irrigant in the list that dissolves organic tissue; it has no effect on inorganic material.

mcqs.q: The wide antimicrobial effect of NaOCl covers:
mcqs.explain: It is also a lubricant and a debriding agent.

mcqs.q: In the chloramination reaction, chlorine released from NaOCl combines with:
opts: Protein amino groups (NH) to form chloramines
mcqs.explain: Free chlorine dissolves necrotic tissue by breaking down proteins into amino acids.

mcqs.q: In the SAPONIFICATION reaction, sodium hypochlorite degrades fatty acids into:
opts: Fatty acid salts (soap) and glycerol, reducing the solution's surface tension
mcqs.explain: Low surface tension is one of the properties of an ideal irrigant, and NaOCl generates it on the spot.

mcqs.q: In the NEUTRALIZATION reaction, sodium hypochlorite neutralizes amino acids by forming:
opts: Water and salt, with the pH reduced as hydroxyl ions exit
mcqs.explain: Saponification deals with fats; neutralization deals with amino acids.

mcqs.q: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) formed when chlorine contacts organic matter is:
opts: A weak acid that acts as an oxidizer
A strong acid that acts as a reducer
mcqs.explain: Hypochlorous acid and hypochlorite ions lead to amino acid degradation and hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: The antimicrobial effectiveness of sodium hypochlorite is based on its high pH, acting through:
mcqs.explain: It is a strong base with a pH greater than 11.

mcqs.q: The effectiveness of NaOCl in cleaning and disinfection depends on:
opts: The concentration of available chlorine and the pH of the solution
The gauge of the needle alone
mcqs.explain: These two variables are what the clinician actually manipulates.

mcqs.q: Which is a disadvantage of sodium hypochlorite?
opts: It is unable to remove the smear layer, because it has no effect on inorganic material
It has no antimicrobial effect on fungi
mcqs.explain: Allergic reaction, unpleasant taste and toxicity are the other three disadvantages.

mcqs.q: If NaOCl is inadvertently extruded through the apex, the classic triad is:
opts: Severe pain, edema, and profuse bleeding from the root canal
Pain, suppuration and sinus tract formation
mcqs.explain: This is why excess pressure and needle binding must be avoided under all circumstances.

mcqs.q: Increasing the temperature of a LOW-concentration NaOCl solution:
opts: Makes it able to remove the smear layer
mcqs.explain: It is one of the three ways of increasing hypochlorite efficacy, with higher concentration and more contact time.

mcqs.q: Higher concentrations of NaOCl are more effective, but:
opts: They are more toxic than lower concentrations
They lose activity against Candida albicans
mcqs.explain: Higher concentrations give better tissue-dissolving ability and are more effective against E. faecalis and C. albicans.

mcqs.q: If a LOWER concentration of NaOCl is used for intracanal irrigation, it should be used:
opts: In higher volume and at more frequent intervals
In lower volume but left in place longer
Mixed with EDTA to restore potency
mcqs.explain: This compensates for the limitations in effectiveness; continuous replenishing and more contact time are the key factors.

mcqs.q: The long-standing effect of chlorhexidine, produced by binding to hydroxyapatite, is called:
mcqs.explain: At low concentrations CHX is adsorbed onto the tooth surface, changing its properties and preventing bacterial colonization.

mcqs.q: The concentration range in which chlorhexidine is used as an endodontic irrigant is:
mcqs.explain: It is a broad spectrum antimicrobial agent with low tissue toxicity compared with NaOCl.

mcqs.q: The principal limitation of chlorhexidine as an irrigant is that it:
opts: Is highly toxic to the periapical tissues
Has a very narrow antimicrobial spectrum
Cannot be used as a final rinse
mcqs.explain: This is exactly the property that makes NaOCl irreplaceable as the key irrigant.

mcqs.q: At HIGH concentrations, chlorhexidine is:
opts: Bactericidal — acting as a detergent, damaging the cell membrane and precipitating the cytoplasm
Bacteriostatic — causing potassium and phosphorus to leak out
mcqs.explain: At LOW concentrations it is bacteriostatic, causing low molecular-weight substances to leak out without permanent damage.

mcqs.q: Chlorhexidine is especially valued because it is effective against:
opts: E. faecalis, which resists NaOCl and calcium hydroxide in failing root-filled teeth
Actinomyces, which resists all other irrigants
mcqs.explain: This is its key clinical niche, particularly in retreatment.

mcqs.q: Mixing NaOCl and CHX produces an orange/brown precipitate of:
mcqs.explain: It is an insoluble neutral salt that occludes dentin tubules and is cytotoxic.

mcqs.q: To avoid the PCA precipitate, after using NaOCl the canal should be:
opts: Dried using paper points before the final CHX rinse
Rinsed with saline and left wet
mcqs.explain: Drying ensures the two solutions never meet inside the canal.

mcqs.q: The suggested regime is to use sodium hypochlorite EXCLUSIVELY in:
opts: All vital and hyperemic canals, taking advantage of its tissue dissolution properties
mcqs.explain: CHX and NaOCl should be used in non-vital teeth and especially in re-treatment cases.

mcqs.q: Decalcifiers (chelators) are defined as chemicals that:
opts: Lower the surface tension of the irrigant
mcqs.explain: They are the chemical answer to the inorganic half of the smear layer, which NaOCl cannot touch.

mcqs.q: EDTA is used in endodontics at a concentration of:
mcqs.explain: It is colorless and chelates the mineralized portion of the smear layer.

mcqs.q: EDTA acts by:
opts: Complexing with the calcium of hydroxyapatite and removing the inorganic smear layer
Breaking proteins down into amino acids
mcqs.explain: It can decalcify to a depth of approximately 50 micrometres.

mcqs.q: EDTA can decalcify to a depth of approximately:
mcqs.explain: Its decalcifying activity is limited to the first several minutes after placement in the canal.

mcqs.q: By itself, EDTA:
opts: Has limited antimicrobial effect, and decalcifies only for the first several minutes
Is strongly antimicrobial and acts for hours
Removes the whole smear layer unaided
mcqs.explain: A proteolytic component such as NaOCl must be added to remove the organic components.

mcqs.q: EDTA and NaOCl should be used SEPARATELY because:
opts: EDTA makes NaOCl lose its tissue-dissolving capacity, leaving virtually no free chlorine
EDTA neutralises the pH of NaOCl to 7
NaOCl prevents EDTA from reaching the canal wall
mcqs.explain: The recommended final flush is EDTA then NaOCl.

mcqs.q: In the final flush, EDTA solution is used:
opts: Once the cleaning and shaping is completed, for around 1 minute
At the very start of instrumentation, for 5 minutes
Only when the canal is calcified
mcqs.explain: It is followed by NaOCl, the two never being mixed together.

mcqs.q: R.C.Prep is a combination of EDTA, polyethylene glycerol base and:
mcqs.explain: It is supplied in a paste form.

mcqs.q: In R.C.Prep, the component that provides ANTISEPTIC properties is:
opts: Urea peroxide, which slowly dissociates into urea and hydrogen peroxide
mcqs.explain: The EDTA provides chelation and the glycerol base provides lubrication.

mcqs.q: The activity of R.C.Prep, like that of EDTA, can be aborted by:
opts: Flooding the canal with 5% sodium hypochlorite solution
mcqs.explain: Its chelating properties otherwise continue to soften dentin.

mcqs.q: MTAD is a mixture of:
opts: Tetracycline antibiotics, citric acid and a detergent
mcqs.explain: The name itself encodes the three components.

mcqs.q: MTAD is recommended in clinical practice:
opts: As a final rinse, after completion of conventional chemo-mechanical preparation
As the primary irrigant throughout instrumentation
mcqs.explain: It is capable of removing both the smear layer and organic tissue.

mcqs.q: QMiX contains a CHX-analog, EDTA as a decalcifying agent, and:
mcqs.explain: It was introduced in 2011 and is used at the end of instrumentation, after NaOCl irrigation.

mcqs.q: In PASSIVE SYRINGE irrigation, the actual exchange of irrigant is restricted to:
opts: 1 to 1.5 mm apical to the needle tip
5 mm apical to the needle tip
mcqs.explain: Fluid dynamics take place near the needle outlet, which is why needle placement matters so much.

mcqs.q: Larger-gauge needles allow quicker and larger fluid exchange, but:
opts: The wider diameter does not allow cleaning of the apical and narrower areas
They increase the risk of tissue dissolution
They cannot be connected to a syringe
mcqs.explain: Placement close to working length guarantees apical exchange, but requires close control to avoid extrusion.

mcqs.q: Special care to prevent irrigant extrusion is needed particularly in:
opts: Immature teeth with wide apical foramina, or when the apical constriction no longer exists
Teeth with a single straight canal
mcqs.explain: Without an apical constriction there is nothing to limit the forward flow of the solution.

mcqs.q: Which is a method of MANUALLY activated irrigation?
opts: Manual push-pull movements using a fitted master gutta-percha cone
Subsonic activation with a polymer tip
mcqs.explain: Corono-apical movements of the needle and stirring with small endodontic instruments are the other two.

mcqs.q: The EndoActivator system uses:
opts: Safe, noncutting polymer tips in a subsonic handpiece
A suction cannula at working length
mcqs.explain: It extrudes a minimal amount of irrigant compared with manual and ultrasonic irrigation.

mcqs.q: Compared with manual syringe irrigation, sonic activation with the EndoActivator:
opts: Renders root canals significantly cleaner, with minimal irrigant extruded out of the apex
Extrudes more irrigant but cleans better
mcqs.explain: Minimal extrusion is specifically noted in comparison with both manual and ultrasonic irrigation.

mcqs.q: Passive ultrasonic irrigation (PUI) is defined by:
opts: The noncutting action of the file and transmission of acoustic energy to the irrigant
The cutting action of an ultrasonic file against the canal wall
Suction applied at the apical third
Subsonic agitation with a polymer tip
mcqs.explain: The word 'passive' refers to the file not cutting dentine.

mcqs.q: PUI should be introduced into the canal:
opts: Once the root canal system has a final apical size and taper
mcqs.explain: It gives better elimination of debris and better penetration of irrigant into the dentinal tubules.

mcqs.q: In negative apical pressure (EndoVac), irrigant is:
opts: Delivered into the access chamber while a suction needle sits in the canal
Injected under high pressure to working length
Agitated with an oscillating ultrasonic file
Delivered through a sealed multisonic platform
mcqs.explain: Because the solution is pulled apically rather than pushed, the direction of flow itself removes the extrusion risk.

mcqs.q: The Gentle Wave system is distinctive because it:
opts: Is non-instrumentational and only requires pulp chamber access
Requires the canal to be prepared to a size 40
Relies on an oscillating file at working length
mcqs.explain: Its multisonic cleaning technology appears able to reach inaccessible canal areas with significantly more cleaned surface than other systems.

saqs.q: State the primary objectives in cleaning and shaping the root canal system.
saqs.a: Remove infected soft and hard tissue · give disinfecting irrigants access to the apical space · create space for medicaments and obturation · retain the integrity of radicular structures.

list: Give disinfecting irrigants access to the apical canal space

saqs.q: Explain the difference between the mechanical and the chemical effectiveness of irrigation.
saqs.a: MECHANICAL — the ability to generate optimum STREAMING FORCES throughout the canal system. CHEMICAL — the CONCENTRATION of the irrigant, the AREA OF CONTACT and the DURATION of interaction with infected material.

head: MECHANICAL effectiveness
CHEMICAL effectiveness
rows: depends on the ability of irrigation to generate optimum STREAMING FORCES within the entire root-canal system
depends on the CONCENTRATION of the antimicrobial irrigant, the AREA OF CONTACT, and the DURATION of the interaction with infected material

saqs.q: List the objectives of irrigation under their three headings.
saqs.a: MECHANICAL and CHEMICAL — flush out debris, lubricate, dissolve organic and inorganic tissue, prevent or dissolve the smear layer. BIOLOGIC — an ANTIMICROBIAL effect.

head: Heading
Objectives
rows: flush out debris · lubricate the canal · dissolve organic and inorganic tissue · prevent the smear layer forming during instrumentation, or dissolve it once formed

saqs.q: Define the smear layer, give its composition, and explain why it is removed in endodontics.
saqs.a: SMEAR LAYER (AAE) — a surface film of debris retained on dentin after instrumentation with rotary instruments or files. COMPOSITION — dentin particles, vital or necrotic pulp remnants, bacterial components, retained irrigant. REMOVED to let irrigants, medications and sealers enter the tubules, and to improve disinfection and filling.

rows: a surface film of debris retained on dentin and other surfaces after instrumentation with rotary instruments or endodontic files
dentin particles · remnants of vital or necrotic pulp tissue · bacterial components · retained irrigant
to let irrigants, medications and sealers penetrate the dentinal tubules, and to improve disinfection and root canal filling

saqs.q: List the five factors affecting the efficiency of root canal irrigation, and give the rules for needle penetration depth.
saqs.a: FIVE FACTORS — needle penetration depth; canal diameter; inner and outer needle diameter; irrigation pressure; type and orientation of the bevel. DEPTH RULES — bend the needle; 2 mm SHORT of working length; lie PASSIVELY and irrigate SLOWLY; NEVER LOCK in the canal; 2 ml each time.

list: Inner and outer diameter of the needle
Place it 2 mm SHORTER than the working length
It must NEVER LOCK in the canal

saqs.q: Give the needle gauge to ISO size conversions, and state the relationship between gauge number and needle width.
saqs.a: 30 g = #30 · 27 g = #40 · 25 g = #50 · 23 g = #60 · 21 g = #80 ISO. The HIGHER the gauge, the NARROWER the needle.

ans.text: The HIGHER the gauge number, the NARROWER the needle — a 30-gauge is finer than a 21-gauge. A common 27-gauge injection needle is 0.42 mm external diameter; irrigation tips of 0.32 mm (30 gauge) are available.

saqs.q: Classify the needle tip designs and explain why the side-vented design is safer.
saqs.a: OPEN-ENDED: (A) flat, (B) beveled, (C) notched. CLOSED-ENDED: (D) side-vented, (E) double side-vented, (F) multi-vented. Side-vented is safer because the CLOSED tip deflects flow sideways through lateral openings instead of jetting straight at the apical foramen.

ans.text: Side-vented needles release the solution through LATERAL OPENINGS and have a CLOSED, SAFE-ENDED TIP — the closed end deflects flow sideways instead of jetting it straight at the apical foramen, which is what makes it safer.

saqs.q: List the properties of an ideal irrigant for root canal treatment.
saqs.a: Effective germicide and fungicide · non-irritating to periapical tissues · stable in solution · prolonged antimicrobial effect · active in blood, serum and protein · low surface tension · does not interfere with repair · non-staining · inactivatable in culture medium · no cell-mediated immune response · removes the smear layer and disinfects tubules · non-antigenic, non-toxic, non-carcinogenic · no adverse effect on dentin or on the seal of filling materials · convenient · inexpensive.

list: Active in the presence of blood, serum and protein
Does not interfere with repair of periapical tissues
Capable of inactivation in a culture medium
Does not induce a cell-mediated immune response
Completely removes the smear layer and disinfects the underlying dentin and tubules
No adverse effect on the physical properties of exposed dentin
No adverse effect on the sealing ability of filling materials

saqs.q: Describe sodium hypochlorite — its concentrations, pH, and why it is the irrigant of choice.
saqs.a: NaOCl is the most used irrigant. Household bleach is 5.25%; pH is ALKALINE 12–13, so it is TISSUE TOXIC and diluted 0.5–5.25%. Irrigant of choice because it dissolves necrotic and vital tissue, organic dentin components and biofilms fast; has a wide antimicrobial range (E. faecalis, Actinomyces, Candida); and acts as a lubricant and debriding agent.

rows: commercial household bleach is 5.25%; used diluted from 0.5% to 5.25% with distilled water to lower toxicity

ans.h: Why it is the irrigant of choice
list: Antibacterial, and dissolves necrotic tissue, vital pulp tissue, the organic components of dentin and biofilms — fast
Acts as a lubricant and debriding agent

saqs.q: Describe the mechanism of action of sodium hypochlorite.
saqs.a: SAPONIFICATION — degrades fatty acids to soap and glycerol, lowering surface tension. NEUTRALIZATION — neutralizes amino acids forming water and salt. CHLORAMINATION — releases chlorine that forms chloramines with protein NH groups, irreversibly inhibiting enzymes. HYPOCHLOROUS ACID — HClO acts as an oxidizer, degrading and hydrolysing amino acids. END RESULT: cell membrane damage, protein denaturation and DNA damage.

head: Mechanism
What happens
rows: acts as an organic and fat solvent, degrading fatty acids into fatty acid salts (soap) and glycerol, reducing surface tension
neutralizes amino acids forming water and salt; with the exit of hydroxyl ions the pH falls
releases chlorine that combines with protein amino (NH) groups to form chloramines — irreversible enzymatic inhibition; free chlorine dissolves necrotic tissue by breaking proteins into amino acids
chlorine dissolving in water with organic matter forms HClO, a weak acid acting as an oxidizer; HClO and hypochlorite ions degrade and hydrolyse amino acids

ans.text: End results — damage to the cell membrane, denaturation of proteins and DNA damage.

saqs.q: List the disadvantages of sodium hypochlorite.
saqs.a: Allergic reaction (hypersensitivity, contact dermatitis) · unpleasant taste · cannot remove the smear layer, having no effect on inorganic material · toxicity — apical extrusion causes severe pain, edema and profuse bleeding.

head: Disadvantage
Detail
rows: hypersensitivity and contact dermatitis, rarely — then use an alternative irrigant of high antimicrobial efficacy
it has no effect on inorganic material
inadvertent extrusion through the apex causes severe accidents — severe pain, edema, and profuse bleeding from the canal

saqs.q: How can the efficacy of hypochlorite preparations be increased?
saqs.a: Increase the TEMPERATURE of low-concentration solutions; use HIGHER CONCENTRATIONS (0.5–5.25%), which dissolve tissue better and are more effective against E. faecalis and C. albicans but are more toxic; and allow MORE CONTACT TIME with continuous replenishment — lower concentrations need higher volume and more frequent intervals.

head: Method
Effect
rows: raising the temperature of low-concentration NaOCl improves immediate tissue-dissolution capacity
better tissue dissolution and more effective against E. faecalis and C. albicans — but more toxic
continuously replenish the solution; with lower concentrations use higher volume at more frequent intervals to compensate

saqs.q: Describe chlorhexidine as an endodontic irrigant, including its concentration-dependent effects.
saqs.a: CHX is broad spectrum, used at 0.2–2%. It binds hydroxyapatite giving SUBSTANTIVITY, completely LACKS tissue-dissolving ability, is less toxic than NaOCl, and lubricates and debrides. HIGH concentration — a DETERGENT, BACTERICIDAL, damaging the membrane and precipitating cytoplasm. LOW — BACTERIOSTATIC, leaking potassium and phosphorus without permanent damage. Very effective against E. faecalis.

ans.text: CHX — a broad spectrum antimicrobial used at 0.2–2%. It binds to hydroxyapatite for a long-standing effect, a property called SUBSTANTIVITY; at low concentrations it adsorbs onto the tooth surface, preventing or reducing bacterial colonization. It completely lacks tissue-dissolving capability, has low tissue toxicity compared with NaOCl, and acts as a lubricant and debriding agent.

head: HIGH concentration
LOW concentration
rows: acts as a DETERGENT and is BACTERICIDAL — damages the cell membrane and precipitates the cytoplasm
BACTERIOSTATIC — low molecular-weight substances such as potassium and phosphorus leak out, without the cell being permanently damaged

ans.text: Very effective against E. faecalis, which resists sodium hypochlorite and calcium hydroxide and is found in failing root-filled teeth.

saqs.q: What happens when NaOCl and CHX are combined, and what is the suggested irrigation regime?
saqs.a: Combining them gives an orange/brown precipitate of PARACHLOROANILINE (PCA), which occludes tubules and is cytotoxic. REGIME: NaOCl exclusively in vital and hyperemic canals; CHX AND NaOCl in non-vital and retreatment cases; NaOCl is the key irrigant with CHX as a FINAL RINSE. Dry with paper points between them so the two never meet.

ans.text: A colour change occurs and an orange/brown precipitate of an insoluble neutral salt forms — PARACHLOROANILINE (PCA). It occludes dentin tubules and is cytotoxic.

list: NaOCl exclusively in all vital and hyperemic canals, using its tissue-dissolution properties
CHX and NaOCl in non-vital teeth, especially re-treatment
NaOCl is the key irrigant; CHX as a FINAL RINSE kills the organisms immune to NaOCl and confers longer-term immunity
After NaOCl, dry with paper points before the CHX rinse — so the two never meet

saqs.q: Describe EDTA and explain how it must be used with NaOCl.
saqs.a: EDTA chelates the MINERALIZED smear layer. Colorless, 17%. It complexes the CALCIUM of hydroxyapatite, softening dentin and decalcifying ~50 µm. Limited antimicrobial effect, active only the first few minutes. It cannot remove the smear layer alone — NaOCl must remove the organic part. But EDTA destroys NaOCl's tissue-dissolving capacity, so use them SEPARATELY: final flush EDTA then NaOCl, ~1 minute, after cleaning and shaping.

rows: chelates and removes the MINERALIZED portion of the smear layer — complexes with the CALCIUM IONS of hydroxyapatite, softening dentin and decalcifying to about 50 µm
limited antimicrobial effect; decalcifying activity lasts only the first several minutes in the canal

ans.text: EDTA alone cannot remove the smear layer — a proteolytic component such as NaOCl is needed for the organic components. However, EDTA causes NaOCl to lose its tissue-dissolving capacity, with virtually no free chlorine in the combination, so the two must be used SEPARATELY. The final flush is EDTA then NaOCl, once cleaning and shaping is complete, for around 1 minute.

saqs.q: Describe R.C.Prep — its composition and advantages.
saqs.a: Lubricants aid file manipulation and initial negotiation in small constricted canals. R.C.PREP = EDTA + urea peroxide + a polyethylene glycerol base, in paste form. Advantages: chelation aids negotiation of constricted canals; the glycerol base lubricates; urea peroxide dissociates to urea and hydrogen peroxide giving antisepsis; activity is aborted by flooding with 5% NaOCl.

ans.text: Lubricants facilitate file manipulation during cleaning and shaping and aid initial canal negotiation, especially in small constricted canals.

list: Chelating properties enhance negotiation of constricted or obliterated canals
The polyethylene glycerol base is a lubricant for instrumentation
Urea peroxide slowly dissociates into urea and hydrogen peroxide, giving antiseptic properties
Its activity, like EDTA's, can be aborted by flooding the canal with 5% NaOCl

saqs.q: Describe MTAD and QMiX.
saqs.a: MTAD = TETRACYCLINE + citric ACID + a DETERGENT; removes BOTH smear layer and organic tissue; a FINAL RINSE after chemo-mechanical preparation; sold as BioPure MTAD, mixed from liquid and powder. QMiX (2011) contains a CHX-analog, TRICLOSAN and EDTA; used at the END of instrumentation, AFTER NaOCl.

head: MTAD
QMiX
rows: removes BOTH the smear layer AND organic tissue from the infected canal system
a FINAL RINSE after conventional chemo-mechanical preparation; sold as BioPure MTAD, mixed from liquid and powder
at the END of instrumentation, AFTER NaOCl irrigation

saqs.q: Describe syringe delivery, its limitations, and the safety rules that apply to it.
saqs.a: In passive syringe irrigation exchange is restricted to 1–1.5 mm APICAL TO THE NEEDLE TIP. Placement near working length is needed for apical exchange, but close control avoids extrusion. Larger gauges exchange more fluid but cannot clean narrow apical areas. SAFETY: never use excess pressure or let the needle bind with no backflow; take special care in immature teeth with wide foramina or a lost constriction.

rows: restricted to 1–1.5 mm apical to the needle tip, the fluid dynamics taking place near the needle outlet
close to working length to guarantee apical exchange — but close control is needed to avoid extrusion
larger gauges give quicker, larger fluid exchange, but the wider diameter cannot clean the apical and narrower areas

list: Avoid excess pressure, and binding of the needle in the canal with no possibility of backflow, under all circumstances
Take special care in immature teeth with wide apical foramina, or when the apical constriction no longer exists, to prevent extrusion

saqs.q: List the six disinfection devices and techniques, and describe manually activated irrigation.
saqs.a: THE SIX: syringe delivery; manually activated; sonically activated; passive ultrasonic; negative apical pressure; Gentle Wave. MANUALLY ACTIVATED — irrigant reaches crevices if AGITATED, by corono-apical movement of the needle, stirring with small instruments, or push-pull with a fitted master gutta-percha cone.

ans.text: MANUALLY ACTIVATED — liquid in the canal reaches crevices and mechanically untouched areas if it is AGITATED, by: corono-apical movements of the irrigation needle · stirring movements with small endodontic instruments · manual push-pull movements with a fitted master gutta-percha cone.

saqs.q: Compare sonically activated irrigation, passive ultrasonic irrigation, negative apical pressure and the Gentle Wave system.
saqs.a: SONIC (EndoActivator) — noncutting polymer tips in a subsonic handpiece; least extrusion, cleaner than manual syringe. PUI — acoustic energy from an oscillating noncutting file; use after final apical size and taper; better debris removal and tubule penetration. NEGATIVE APICAL PRESSURE (EndoVac) — suction PULLS solution apically rather than pushing. GENTLE WAVE — multisonic, non-instrumentational, needs only chamber access; reaches inaccessible areas.

head: System
How it works and what it gives
rows: safe, noncutting polymer tips in a subsonic handpiece agitate the irrigant quickly and vigorously — minimal extrusion compared with manual and ultrasonic, and canals significantly cleaner than manual syringe irrigation

the noncutting action of an ultrasonically activated file transmits acoustic energy from the oscillating file to the irrigant. Introduce once the canal has its final apical size and taper — better debris elimination and better penetration into the tubules
irrigant is delivered into the access chamber and a very fine needle connected to the suction is placed in the canal, so the solution is pulled rather than pushed apically
multisonic cleaning technology; non-instrumentational, requiring only pulp chamber access, and able to reach inaccessible canal areas with significantly more cleaned surface
